lessons.title: Sourcing and Preparing Local Scrap Steel in Africa
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 3, Lesson 1 of the Yok and Pan Blacksmith training. In this lesson we focus on the single most important input for your forge: steel. In many African towns, the best steel is not bought new from a factory. It is recovered from scrap yards, mechanic workshops, old vehicles, broken farm tools, and construction sites. Your ability to identify, sort, and prepare this steel determines the quality of every pan, hoe, knife, hinge, and tool you sell. Start by building relationships with three types of suppliers: mechanics who replace leaf springs and axles, construction foremen who discard rebar and angle iron, and market traders who collect broken implements. Pay small deposits or offer free sharpening in exchange for first pick. Always carry a magnet and a small file. The magnet tells you if steel is ferrous. The file tells you hardness. A file that bites easily means mild steel, good for decorative work. A file that skates means high carbon steel, good for cutting edges. Leaf springs from trucks and buses are the blacksmith gold of Africa. They are usually 5160 or similar spring steel, tough and hardenable. Coil springs from cars work too but require more forging. Axles are thick and good for anvils, hammers, and heavy chisels. Rebar is mild steel, useful for tongs, fire tools, and structural pieces but not for knives that must hold an edge. Old files and rashers are high carbon and excellent for small blades, punches, and chisels. Saw blades from timber mills are another treasure, often high carbon and thin. Avoid galvanized steel because the zinc coating releases toxic fumes when heated. Avoid painted or plastic-coated metal unless you can grind or burn it off safely outdoors. Avoid steel with unknown alloys that spark strangely or crack under the hammer. Once you collect scrap, sort it into three piles: high carbon for edges, medium carbon for tools, and mild steel for structure. Label each pile with paint or tags. Store under a roof to prevent rust. Before forging, cut pieces to manageable lengths using a hacksaw, angle grinder, or hot cut. Remove rust with a wire brush or a vinegar bath. Vinegar is cheap and available in most African markets. Soak rusty steel for 12 to 24 hours, then scrub and dry. For heavy rust, use a dilute hydrochloric acid bath outdoors with gloves and goggles, then neutralize with baking soda and rinse. Never use acid indoors. Annealing is the next step for high carbon steel. Heat the steel to a dull red, about 700 to 750 degrees Celsius, then bury it in dry wood ash, lime, or vermiculite and let it cool slowly overnight. This softens the steel so you can file, drill, and shape it. Without annealing, high carbon steel will crack or dull your tools. For medium carbon steel, a simple normalizing cycle is enough: heat to red, remove from fire, and let it cool in still air. This relieves stress from the scrap yard. Keep a logbook for every batch of steel. Record the source, date, magnet test, file test, spark test, and heat treatment. The spark test is a practical field skill. Touch the steel to a grinding wheel in a dark area. Long yellow sparks with few bursts mean low carbon. Short orange sparks with many starbursts mean high carbon. This helps you separate mystery steel without a laboratory. In Africa, where formal steel certification is rare, your logbook becomes your quality control. Price your products to reflect steel quality. A knife from a known leaf spring can sell for three times the price of a knife from rebar. Teach your customers this difference. Show them the spark test and the file test. Build trust by stamping your mark on every high carbon blade. Finally, think about supply security. Scrap prices rise when construction booms. Build a stockpile of at least three months of high carbon steel. Train a young apprentice to sort and clean scrap. Pay suppliers fairly and on time. In many communities, the blacksmith who respects scrap dealers becomes the first to receive the best leaf springs and axles. Your forge is only as good as your steel. Treat sourcing as a business skill, not a chore. In the next lesson, we will design and build a fuel-efficient African forge that uses charcoal, coal, or even agricultural waste.

lessons.title: Building a Fuel-Efficient Forge for African Conditions
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 3, Lesson 2. A forge is the heart of your blacksmith business. In Africa, you must build a forge that works with local fuels, local materials, and local weather. This lesson gives you practical designs for a fuel-efficient forge that uses charcoal, coal, or biomass briquettes. The goal is simple: reach welding heat with less fuel, less smoke, and less time. Start with the firepot. The firepot is a shallow bowl where the fire burns. It should be made of thick steel, cast iron, or fired clay. A good size is 25 to 30 centimeters across and 10 to 15 centimeters deep. A deeper pot wastes fuel. A shallower pot loses heat. You can make a firepot from an old brake drum, a truck wheel rim, or a steel plate welded into a box. Line it with clay mixed with sand and a little cement. This lining protects the metal and holds heat. The tuyere is the pipe that brings air into the fire. It should enter the firepot from the side, about 5 centimeters above the bottom. Use a 5 centimeter steel pipe. Angle it slightly downward so ash does not clog it. The air source can be a hand-cranked blower, a bellows made from goat skin, or a small electric fan powered by a solar panel or car battery. In many African workshops, a 12 volt computer fan or a car heater blower works well. Connect it with a dimmer switch or a valve so you can control air flow. Too much air burns steel and wastes fuel. Too little air gives a cold fire. The forge table surrounds the firepot. It should be about 60 by 60 centimeters, made of steel plate or packed clay. The table holds the fire and gives you a place to rest tools. Slope the table slightly toward the firepot so coal or charcoal feeds itself as it burns. Add a water trough at one side for cooling tongs and quenching. Add a tool rack at the other side for hammers, chisels, and punches. For the fuel, charcoal is the most common in Africa. It burns clean and reaches welding heat quickly. But charcoal is expensive and often causes deforestation. Make your own charcoal from agricultural waste: maize cobs, rice husks, coconut shells, groundnut shells, and sawdust. Build a simple retort kiln from a 200 liter drum. Fill it with dry biomass, seal it, and heat it from below. The gases burn off and you are left with charcoal. This saves money and reduces smoke. Coal is better for long forging sessions because it lasts longer and produces a reducing fire that protects steel from oxidation. If you can get coal, mix it with charcoal at a 50 50 ratio. This gives you the best of both fuels. Never use wet coal or wet charcoal. Store fuel under a roof. A fuel-efficient forge also needs a hood and chimney. Smoke and carbon monoxide are serious health risks. Build a hood from sheet metal or clay. Shape it like an inverted funnel above the fire. Connect it to a chimney pipe that rises at least 2 meters above the roof. The chimney creates draft and pulls smoke away from your lungs. If you cannot build a chimney, forge outdoors or in a well-ventilated shed with open sides. Never forge in a closed room. Now let us talk about fire management. Start with a small fire. Add fuel gradually. Keep the fire in a mound shape, not a flat bed. The mound concentrates heat. Use a rake or a poker to keep the firepot clear. Remove clinker and ash regularly. Clinker is melted impurities that block air flow. In a charcoal fire, clinker is less of a problem. In a coal fire, remove clinker every 30 minutes. Control the fire with air and fuel, not with water. Water creates steam and cools the fire. If you need a smaller fire, reduce air and stop adding fuel. For welding heat, you need a bright yellow white fire. For forging heat, a bright orange fire is enough. For annealing, a dull red fire works. Learn to read the fire by color. In daylight, use a shade or a piece of dark glass to judge color accurately. Build a second forge for heat treating. This can be a simple charcoal trench or a small gas forge. A gas forge uses propane or butane and gives precise temperature control. In Africa, gas can be expensive and cylinders are not always available. But for high value knives and tools, a gas forge pays for itself because it reduces oxidation and gives consistent hardness. If you cannot afford gas, use a charcoal forge with a muffle pipe. A muffle pipe is a steel pipe closed at one end. Place the blade inside the pipe and heat the pipe in the forge. This protects the blade from direct fire and gives even heat. Finally, maintain your forge. Replace clay lining when it cracks. Clean the tuyere. Check the blower bearings. Keep a spare fan and a spare pipe. Train your apprentices to respect the forge. A well-built forge can last ten years. A poorly built forge wastes fuel, ruins steel, and damages your health. In the next lesson, we will cover hammer techniques and anvil work for African pan and tool production.

lessons.title: Hammer Technique and Anvil Work for African Products
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 3, Lesson 3. In this lesson we focus on the physical skills that turn steel into sellable products. You will learn hammer technique, anvil work, and the specific sequences for making pans, hoes, knives, and hinges. These are the products that sell in African markets. Start with your stance. Stand close to the anvil with your feet shoulder width apart. Your hammer hand is your dominant hand. Your tong hand holds the steel. Keep your elbows slightly bent. Do not lock your knees. Breathe out when you strike. A blacksmith who holds his breath tires quickly. Grip the hammer near the end of the handle. A loose grip gives more speed. A tight grip gives more control. Learn both. For heavy blows, use a loose grip and let the hammer head do the work. For precise blows, choke up on the handle and use a tight grip. The anvil should be at knuckle height. If it is too high, you lose power. If it is too low, you bend your back. Mount the anvil on a hardwood stump or a steel stand filled with sand. Sand reduces noise and vibration. Secure the anvil with chains or bolts. A moving anvil wastes energy and damages your work. Now let us cover the basic hammer blows. The first is the flat blow. This is used for drawing out, flattening, and straightening. Strike with the full face of the hammer. Keep your wrist stiff. The second is the peen blow. The peen is the rounded or wedge-shaped end. Use it for spreading metal, making curves, and moving metal in one direction. The third is the glancing blow. This is used for bending and offsetting. Strike at an angle so the metal moves sideways. The fourth is the controlled blow. This is a light tap used for final shaping and setting rivets. Practice each blow on mild steel until it becomes automatic. Draw out a piece of rebar into a taper. Then draw it back into a square. Then draw it into a point. Repeat until you can control the shape without thinking. For African pan production, start with a flat disc of mild steel or recycled plow blade. Heat the disc to bright orange. Place it on a shallow dish or a wooden stump with a hollow. Use a ball peen hammer to sink the center. Work in circles from the center outward. Reheat often. Do not let the steel go below cherry red. If it cools, it cracks. Once the pan has a bowl shape, planish it with a flat hammer over a stake or anvil horn. Planishing removes hammer marks and smooths the surface. Then trim the rim with a hot cut or a chisel. Finally, grind the rim smooth and drill holes for a handle if needed. A good cooking pan takes about two hours of forging. It sells well in local markets and to restaurants. For hoes, start with a leaf spring or a piece of medium carbon steel. Cut a rectangle about 20 centimeters by 15 centimeters. Heat and draw out the blade to a trapezoid shape. The cutting edge should be thinner than the back. Use a hot cut to shape the sides. Then bend the socket or eye. The eye is where the handle fits. You can form the eye by splitting the back of the blade and wrapping it around a mandrel. Weld the seam with a forge weld or a modern welder. Then heat treat the blade. Quench the cutting edge in oil or water, then temper it in an oven or over a fire until it turns straw yellow. A good hoe lasts for years and sells for a good price. For knives, start with a high carbon file or leaf spring. Draw out the blade. Keep the spine thick and the edge thin. Forge the tang. Normalize the blade three times to relieve stress. Then anneal it in ash. File and grind the bevels. Heat treat by heating the blade to non-magnetic, then quenching in warm oil. Temper at 200 degrees Celsius for one hour. This gives a hard edge and a tough spine. For hinges, use mild steel. Draw out a strap. Roll the eye around a pin. Forge the pin. Assemble and rivet. Hinges sell to carpenters and builders. They are simple and repeatable. In Africa, repeatable products build your reputation. Make ten hinges that are identical. Then make twenty. Standardize your sizes. Use jigs and gauges. A jig is a simple fixture that holds metal in place. A gauge is a marked stick or plate that shows length and angle. With jigs and gauges, you can train apprentices faster and reduce waste. Finally, think about safety. Wear leather gloves when handling hot steel. Wear safety glasses when grinding. Keep your hammer handle tight. Never strike two hammers together. Never use a hammer with a cracked handle. Keep water and oil away from the fire. In the next lesson, we will cover heat treatment and quality control for African tools.

lessons.title: Heat Treatment and Quality Control for African Tools
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 3, Lesson 4. Heat treatment is the difference between a tool that works and a tool that fails. In Africa, customers remember a knife that dulls quickly or a hoe that chips. This lesson gives you practical heat treatment methods using local materials and simple quality control steps. Start with the three stages of heat treatment: normalizing, annealing, and hardening and tempering. Normalizing means heating steel to a dull red and letting it cool in still air. This relieves stress from forging. Do it three times for high carbon steel. Annealing means heating steel to a dull red and cooling it very slowly in ash, lime, or vermiculite. This softens the steel so you can file and drill it. Hardening means heating steel to its critical temperature and quenching it quickly. Tempering means reheating the hardened steel to a lower temperature to reduce brittleness. The critical temperature is the point where steel becomes non-magnetic. Use a magnet to test. Heat the steel until the magnet no longer sticks. That is the critical temperature. For most high carbon steels, this is around 750 to 800 degrees Celsius. In daylight, this is a bright cherry red. In dark conditions, it is a dull orange. Do not rely on color alone. Use a magnet. For quenching, you need a quench tank. A metal bucket or a plastic drum works. For oil quenching, use clean motor oil, vegetable oil, or used cooking oil. Warm the oil to about 50 degrees Celsius. Cold oil can crack thin blades. Hot oil can catch fire. For water quenching, use clean water at room temperature. Water is faster than oil and can crack high carbon steel. Use water only for simple steels like 1080 or 1095. Use oil for alloy steels like 5160 from leaf springs. When quenching, plunge the blade into the oil edge first, then move it in a figure eight pattern. Do not move it side to side. That can warp the blade. Hold it in the oil until it stops smoking, about 10 to 15 seconds. Then remove it and check for hardness with a file. A file should skate across the edge. If the file bites, the blade did not harden. Reheat and try again. After hardening, the blade is too brittle. You must temper it. Temper in a kitchen oven, a charcoal fire, or a gas torch. For knives, temper at 200 degrees Celsius for one hour. For hoes and axes, temper at 230 to 250 degrees Celsius for one hour. For springs and chisels, temper at 280 to 300 degrees Celsius. If you do not have a thermometer, use color. Clean the steel with sandpaper. Heat it slowly. Watch the oxide colors. Straw yellow is about 200 degrees. Brown is about 240 degrees. Purple is about 280 degrees. Blue is about 300 degrees. For knives, stop at straw yellow. For hoes, stop at brown. For springs, stop at purple. Quench again in oil to stop the tempering process. Now let us talk about quality control. Every batch of tools should be tested. Test one piece from each batch. For knives, cut a piece of hardwood 50 times. The edge should still shave hair or cut paper. For hoes, chop into a piece of dry soil or a small branch. The edge should not chip or roll. For hinges, open and close them 100 times. They should not squeak or loosen. Keep a record of every batch. Write down the steel source, the hardening temperature, the quench medium, the tempering temperature, and the test results. If a batch fails, you can trace the problem. In Africa, where customers talk to each other, one bad tool can ruin your reputation. One good tool can bring ten new customers. Also, think about surface finish. A rough surface rusts faster. Grind and polish your tools. For knives, polish to at least 400 grit. For hoes, leave a forged finish but remove scale. For hinges, paint or oil them to prevent rust. Use local materials for finishing. Palm oil, shea butter, and beeswax make good rust preventatives. Mix beeswax with a little oil and rub it on warm steel. It gives a nice finish and protects against humidity. Finally, train your apprentices in heat treatment. Do not let them guess. Give them a magnet, a thermometer, and a logbook. Teach them to test every batch. A blacksmith who controls heat treatment controls quality. A blacksmith who controls quality controls the market. In the next lesson, we will cover pricing, marketing, and scaling your blacksmith business in Africa.

lessons.title: Pricing, Marketing, and Scaling Your Blacksmith Business
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 3, Lesson 5. You have learned to source steel, build a forge, hammer products, and heat treat them. Now you must sell them at a profit and grow your business. This lesson covers pricing, marketing, and scaling in an African context. Start with costing. You must know the true cost of every product. List your costs: steel, fuel, labor, rent, tools, transport, and marketing. Add 10 percent for waste and breakage. Add 20 percent for profit. That is your minimum price. Do not guess. Use a notebook. For example, a knife from a leaf spring may use 500 shillings of steel, 300 shillings of charcoal, 200 shillings of oil and sandpaper, and 2 hours of labor at 500 shillings per hour. That is 2000 shillings. Add 10 percent waste, 200 shillings. Add 20 percent profit, 440 shillings. Your price is 2640 shillings. Round up to 2700 shillings. If the market price is lower, you must reduce costs or improve quality. Do not sell at a loss. Many African blacksmiths underprice their work because they do not count their labor. Your labor is valuable. Pay yourself first. Next, segment your market. In most African towns, you have four customer groups: households, farmers, builders, and traders. Households buy cooking pans, knives, and fire tools. Farmers buy hoes, machetes, and sickles. Builders buy hinges, nails, and window frames. Traders buy in bulk and resell at markets. Each group has different needs. Households care about price and durability. Farmers care about edge retention and handle fit. Builders care about standard sizes and fast delivery. Traders care about margin and repeatability. Create different product lines for each group. For households, make a low cost pan and a high end pan. For farmers, make a standard hoe and a premium hoe. For builders, make hinges in three standard sizes. For traders, offer a discount for orders of ten or more. Now let us talk about marketing. In Africa, word of mouth is the strongest marketing. But you can accelerate it. First, make a signboard. Paint your business name and what you make. Put it where people pass. Second, use your products as advertisements. Stamp your mark on every tool. Give a small discount to customers who bring a friend. Third, go to markets. Set up a stall one day a week. Demonstrate your tools. Cut a piece of wood with a knife. Chop a branch with a hoe. Let people feel the balance. Fourth, work with local institutions. Schools, clinics, and NGOs buy tools in bulk. Write a simple letter. Offer a discount for bulk orders. Fifth, use mobile phones. Take photos of your products. Send them to customers on WhatsApp. Create a simple catalog. List your prices. Sixth, train apprentices who become ambassadors. When they start their own forges, they send you customers. Now let us talk about scaling. Scaling means making more products without losing quality. The first step is standardization. Choose five products that sell best. Make them in batches of ten or twenty. Use jigs and gauges. The second step is division of labor. One apprentice cuts steel. One heats and forges. One grinds and finishes. One handles sales. This increases output. The third step is inventory. Keep a stock of finished goods. Do not wait for orders. When a customer comes, you have the product ready. The fourth step is a second forge. Build a second forge in a different market. Put a trusted apprentice in charge. Visit weekly. Share profits. The fifth step is diversification. Add products that use the same skills: garden tools, door handles, bicycle parts, and art pieces. The sixth step is record keeping. Track your sales, expenses, and profits every week. Know which products make money and which do not. Cut the losers. Grow the winners. Finally, think about the future. In Africa, the demand for quality tools is growing. Construction, farming, and tourism all need blacksmith products. You can also export. African handmade knives and art pieces sell online. But exporting requires consistent quality, packaging, and paperwork. Start local. Build your reputation. Then expand. Remember, your business is not just about making things. It is about solving problems. A farmer needs a hoe that does not break. A cook needs a pan that heats evenly. A builder needs a hinge that lasts. When you solve problems, customers pay. When you pay yourself, you stay in business. When you train others, you build a legacy. This concludes Module 3. You now have the practical skills to source steel, build a forge, forge products, heat treat them, and sell them at a profit. Go and build your business. Your community needs your skills.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of tempering steel after hardening in blacksmithing?
options: A) To increase hardness and brittleness
B) To reduce brittleness and relieve internal stresses
C) To change the steel color permanently
D) To remove all carbon from the surface
quiz.explanation: Tempering reduces brittleness and relieves internal stresses created during hardening, improving toughness.

quiz.q: Which color indicates the steel has reached approximately 400 degrees Fahrenheit during tempering?
quiz.explanation: Light straw appears around 400 degrees Fahrenheit and is used for tools needing high hardness.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the blacksmithing heat treatment process?
quiz.explanation: The typical sequence is annealing to soften, hardening to increase hardness, then tempering to reduce brittleness.

quiz.q: Which quenching medium produces the fastest cooling rate for steel?
quiz.explanation: Brine cools faster than water, oil, or air, making it suitable for certain shallow-hardening steels.

quiz.q: What happens to steel if it is quenched in water instead of oil when oil is recommended?
options: A) It may crack or warp due to too rapid cooling
B) It will become softer than desired
C) It will not harden at all
D) It will turn into cast iron
quiz.explanation: Water quenches faster than oil and can cause excessive stress, leading to cracks or warping.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of normalizing steel in blacksmithing?
options: A) To harden the steel for cutting tools
B) To refine grain structure and relieve internal stresses
C) To add a protective coating to the surface
D) To increase the carbon content of the steel
quiz.explanation: Normalizing refines grain structure and relieves internal stresses by air cooling after heating.

quiz.q: Which test is commonly used to check if steel has reached the correct hardening temperature?
quiz.explanation: Steel becomes non-magnetic at its critical temperature, so the magnet test helps confirm hardening temperature.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of overheating steel during forging or heat treatment?
options: A) It becomes too soft to forge
D) It may burn, causing grain growth and weakness
quiz.explanation: Overheating can burn steel, causing excessive grain growth and making the metal weak and brittle.
